chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: The 1934 Decca session of old tunes
summary: Hines's idea to revive Maple Leaf Rag, Wolverine Blues.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Yeah. Let's move back to 1934. There's a recording date, for Decca, I believe it is, it's been reissued on Decca. There were several old tunes recorded like "Maple Leaf Rag" and "Copenhagen".
Yeah.
"That's a Plenty," "Wolverine Blues," "Sweet Georgia Brown," and on those last two, you
made those nice arrangements.
Yeah.
This was sort of a departure from what the band had been recording up to then. The tunes.
Uh-huh.
Do you recall whose idea that was, to record that thing?
I think that was Earl's.
Earl?
Yeah.
Obviously he thought there was some commercial value.
Commercial value, yeah.
Did the record sell well?
Yeah, it sold well. See, because them are the sort of tunes we used to play years ago when I first started back in the twenties.
Right. That's -- part of the traditional --
Yeah, he figured we'd revive them, you know. They went real well.
Yeah, I really like that sax solo you wrote on 'Sweet Georgia Brown.' Very much like Fletcher Henderson -- the things that Fletcher Henderson --
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
It's really nice. And Earl just played his tail off. Like "Maple Leaf Rag," which is sort of not his standard repertoir.
No.
But did you play those arrangements out at the club, too?
Yeah, everything we recorded, we played at the club. At dances, on one-nighters, on the road.
